title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription software was deployed to record meetings on video conferencing platforms with settings that allegedly recorded and transmitted conversations to the company by default, without clear notification to all participants. The deployment appears to have lacked adequate consent mechanisms, with participants discovering after the fact that their conversations were being captured and used for AI training without their knowledge or agreement.

This represents a failure in system transparency and consent architecture. A transcription service that processes sensitive workplace conversations should require explicit opt-in from all participants before recording begins, not rely on default settings or permission boxes that users may not encounter or understand. Human review of consent practices before deployment, or safeguards that prevent recording unless all parties have actively confirmed permission, would have caught this gap.

It is not established whether the company intentionally misled users or whether technical design simply failed to implement adequate consent. The lawsuit alleges violations of privacy and wiretap law, but such allegations remain subject to court proceedings and are not yet proven findings.

Otter.ai faces class action lawsuit for unauthorized meeting recording
Enterprise note-taking apps face legal scrutiny as Otter hit with privacy suit

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The company's software, which transcribes meetings on Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams, allegedly records discussions by default and shares them with Otter to improve its artificial intelligence systems without adequately notifying participants. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter was covertly recording confidential conversations. The suit alleges the practice violates state and federal privacy and wiretap laws and seeks class-action status to represent other California users whose conversations were unknowingly shared with the company for financial gain.

Otter.ai, which serves approximately 25 million users and has processed over 1 billion meetings since 2016, claims its privacy policy discloses that user data is used for training purposes when users check a permission box. However, the lawsuit contends many users are still misled. Recent complaints on social media reveal concerns about the software automatically joining meetings linked to workplace calendars and recording conversations without participant consent. The suit also questions whether Otter's method of anonymizing data before feeding it into machine learning systems is effective, noting the company provides no public explanation of its deidentification process.
